title: Mould prevention and concealed damage
audience: Coordinators, supervisors and trained workers who may be asked about, triage, refer or document cleaning and water-removal work after a flood or water event. Not a qualification or authority to enter a flood-affected building, energise its systems, or certify it as dry, safe or habitable.
learningOutcomes: Recognise hidden microbial contamination and concealed damage, and refer rather than disturb suspect material to prove a point.

instruction.heading: Scope and authority
instruction.body: This lesson teaches how to recognise signs of possible hidden microbial contamination and concealed damage, and how to refer them. It does not identify organisms, test for microbes or certify a space as free of contamination. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instruction.heading: Mould prevention and concealed damage
instruction.body: Musty odour, staining, repeated moisture events and concealed cavities can signal conditions that need specialist investigation. Do not disturb suspect materials in order to prove a hypothesis. File a hidden-damage referral that records the scope exclusions and the route for notifying the occupants. Pause the normal restoration work and escalate any suspected hidden microbial contamination to a competent professional. Occupant communication must be factual and must not state that the building is safe.

procedure: Record any musty odour, staining, repeated moisture events and concealed cavities.
Pause normal restoration work in the affected area.
Do not disturb suspect material to prove a suspicion.
File a hidden-damage referral that records the scope exclusions.
Escalate any suspected hidden microbial contamination to a competent professional.
Tell occupants the facts, the scope exclusions and the referral route, without saying that the building is safe.

workedExamples.situation: After a flood, a tenant reports a musty smell behind a recently repainted wall.
workedExamples.reasoning: Pause work in the area, file a hidden-damage referral and do not open the wall to prove the suspicion. Tell the tenant the facts and the referral route.

workedExamples.situation: A crew proposes to paint over a stain that appeared after the flood, so the room looks finished.
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Painting does not remove the cause and hides the evidence. Record and refer the stain first.

equipmentAndPpe: Exposure controls set by the hazard assessment for the area. See the PPE and hygiene lesson.

commonErrors.error: Opening a wall to prove a suspicion.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not disturb suspect material. Refer it for investigation.
Paint does not remove the source. Record and refer.

commonErrors.error: Telling occupants that the building is safe.
commonErrors.prevention: State the facts and the referral. Do not give a safety statement.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This lesson does not identify or test for microbes and does not clear a space. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.
Occupant communication about possible contamination must be factual.

qualityStandard: The learner pauses work and refers suspect hidden damage.
The learner does not disturb suspect material to prove a hypothesis.
documentationEvidence: Hidden-damage referral with the scope exclusions and the occupant notification route.
summary: A musty smell and staining are warning signs.
Do not state that the building is safe.

knowledgeChecks.question: Musty odour and staining appear behind a wall after a flood. What should be done?
options: Open the wall to see the problem, since the crew needs to know exactly what is happening behind it
Refer the concealed damage for specialist investigation and do not disturb suspect material to prove a hypothesis.
Paint over the staining, since the paint will seal the wall and stop the smell from coming through

knowledgeChecks.question: A tenant asks whether a repainted room is now safe. What is correct?
options: Yes, the paint seals the problem
Say the room is safe because the stain is hidden
Give a factual scope and refer the safety question to a competent professional. Do not state the building is safe.

moduleAuthority.heading: Module authority and restricted work
moduleAuthority.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to enter a flood-affected building, to carry out regulated flood restoration, to energise or isolate electrical, gas or solar systems, to remove sewage or contaminated water, to dispose of waste, or to certify that a property is dry, hygienic, structurally sound or safe to occupy. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate or approval. Some of the work described is restricted to licensed, authorised or specially trained people, including electrical and gas work, structural assessment, sewage handling and some disposal. The site controller, the owner, the insurer and the competent professionals each hold separate decisions, and none of them replaces the others. Where the controlling authority or the competent professional is not identified, stop and refer.

stopWorkAndReferral.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
stopWorkAndReferral.body: Stop and refer whenever any of these is true: permission to enter or written safety clearance is missing; the contamination is unknown; a structural hazard, a slip or a confined space has not been cleared; an electrical, gas or solar system is water-exposed or has not been licensed for re-energisation; an exposure has occurred or controls are not in place; the equipment or operators are not suitable; porous material is in question; hidden microbial contamination is suspected; a waste route is not yet known; or a party asks for a dry, hygienic or occupancy statement. A stop-work decision is correct. Record it, and restart only after the competent party has confirmed the scope in writing.
